newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Heinz chief O'Reilly seen planning slow exit.
newsitem.headline: Heinz chief O'Reilly seen planning slow exit.

text.p: The boss of H.J. Heinz, Irish entrepreneur Anthony O'Reilly, plans a slow exit from the multinational corporation, sources close to the company said on Tuesday.
Heinz president William Johnson is tipped as the front runner in the race to succeed the 61-year-old former international rugby star.
Johnson, appointed president of the group in 1996, has been challenged with the task of orchestrating the food group's restructuring and O'Reilly's departure depends on how well it goes.

"I think you are looking at another two to three years before he (O'Reilly) retires. Johnson is only president for a year and it all depends on how successful the restructuring is," a source close to the company said.

Heinz will reveal the details of its restructuring plan on Friday to analysts in San Francisco, the source said, adding that he thought it highly unlikely that O'Reilly would make any statement on his retirement at the meeting.
"Rumours that O'Reilly will use the meeting to announce his retirement plans are just that, rumours," the source said.

"There has been speculation for some time that O'Reilly would retire from Heinz and concentrate more of his time on his considerable Irish interests," one analyst said, noting that O'Reilly, who likes to take a hands-on approach to his businesses, has interests spanning five continents.
This speculation heightened last year when O'Reilly was rumoured to be in ill-health. O'Reilly later denied that his health was a source of concern.

What drives a multi-millionaire married to a shipping heiress -- Chryss Goulandris -- who mixes with multi-millionaires at his palatial home outside Dublin, at the Deauville race track in France and in Manhattan.
"It's the Tony Who factor," said a contemporary. "Someone once said Tony Who when his name was mentioned. He doesn't like that. He wants people to know who Tony O'Reilly is."

O'Reilly's flagship Irish company, 400 million Irish pound media group Independent Newspapers Plc has become a serious international player in media and communications with interests in Australia, South Africa and New Zealand to name but a few.

O'Reilly's 150 million punt industrial holding company Fitzwilton Plc has a share register which reads like a who's who for the rich and famous while his exploration group ARCON International Resources Plc says it expects promising results from a lead and zinc mine in the Irish midlands. O'Reilly is also chairman of crystal and china group Waterford Wedgwood Plc.

Thirty years ago he was a household name as a rugby star who began playing for his country at the age of 19, went on to play 29 times for Ireland and set a 1959 scoring record in New Zealand and Australia that still stands.
Old photographs show him outstretched, ball in hand, leaving the clutching arms of would-be interceptors in his wake.
"Ireland is a great place to tog out in (put on your sports kit), but you have to play the big game elsehwere," is an oft-quoted O'Reilly remark.

These days the photos show a greyer, less harried man togged out in black dinner suit or jacket and tie at a celebrity dinner in Manhattan or at breakfast with Henry Kissinger. Outside of Ireland he is less well-known, despite a meteoric career of 30 years. Perhaps that is what drives him.
In 1970, at the venerable age of 34, he was recalled to play for Ireland and was driven to practice in a black limousine, often asleep. He was already head of Heinz in Britain.
He was elected president and Chief Execuive officer of Heinz in June 1979 and became Chairman in 1987.
